clue.text: Last year's winner not skating - he's got a job

blocks.note: someone not skating is off the ice, read as OFF ICE
the reigning champion holds the title until it is next contested

explanation.surface: A former champion has given up the rink for paid employment.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the opposite order to the clue: the skating part, OFF ICE, goes first and HOLDER after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An officeholder holds a post or position, so he is a person with an appointed role or employment.

clue.text: Bunting from church door to lancet window

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows, spanning several of them

blocks.note: surface padding: sets the scene inside a church
the letters run across the end of door, all of to and the start of lancet
surface padding: a lancet is a narrow pointed window

explanation.surface: A small bird flits through a church, from its door to a pointed window.
explanation.definitionFit: The ortolan is a small European songbird of the bunting family, famously eaten as a delicacy in France.

clue.text: See 22
It appears in the spring of an antelope in a moving start

indicators.note: in places the animal inside the word for the moving start, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: cine is the start of words for moving pictures, as in cinema and cine camera
the eland is a large African antelope

explanation.surface: A leaping antelope's spring, as it bolts from a standing start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the antelope's leap but is the season. Cine is the familiar British prefix for film cameras and home movies.
explanation.definitionFit: The lesser celandine is a yellow wild flower that blooms early each spring in woods and hedgerows.

clue.text: Laughs like dry moats

blocks.note: first meaning: bursts of laughter written out as sounds
second meaning: sunken ditches that bound a park without blocking the view

explanation.surface: Someone compares laughter to empty moats around a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha-ha is a sunken ditch and wall used on British country estates to keep livestock out without a visible fence.
explanation.definitionFit: A ha-ha is a landscape-garden trench acting as a hidden barrier, so plural ha-has are like waterless moats; the same letters are also chuckles.

clue.text: Shearers' party hit the hay

blocks.note: to lam is to beat or thrash
hay is packed into a bale

explanation.surface: After the shearing party everyone goes off to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit the hay' looks like the idiom for going to bed, but it is read word by word.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamb-ale was a traditional rural feast held at lamb-shearing time, with ale drunk in celebration.

clue.text: 10 with real potential never finishing

indicators.note: potential describes what letters could become once rearranged, not what they now spell

blocks.note: the number written out as a word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something with real potential that never quite gets completed.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 looks like a cross-reference to 10 Down, but here it is just the number ten spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal means lasting for ever, without end, which is the same as never finishing.

clue.text: Bookmaker required? I doubt it

blocks.note: first meaning: if a bookie is needed, the punter wishes to place a wager
second meaning: a sceptical retort challenging what someone has just said

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: needing a bookmaker means wanting to bet, read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a colloquial retort expressing disbelief, inviting the speaker to wager on their claim.

clue.text: Work to amuse the audience could be an illusion

indicators.note: an audience hears the words, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: OP is short for opus, a musical work
to tickle is to amuse

explanation.surface: A comic piece written to entertain an audience might be a mere trick.
explanation.walkthrough: OP plus a word that sounds like TICKLE gives OPTICAL.
explanation.definitionFit: An optical illusion is a visual trick, so the word could stand before illusion; the definition gestures at that phrase.

clue.text: Emphatically he who could be Flemish...

indicators.note: could be says the letters may turn into something else, once rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man stressed as someone who might turn out to be from Flanders; the dots run into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Himself is the emphatic or reflexive form of the pronoun, as in 'he did it himself'.

clue.text: Playtime for piano among stringed instruments, final heats

indicators.note: among puts one item in the midst of a group, so the letter goes inside

blocks.note: split in two: play is fun and a time is an era
lyres are ancient harps
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: Children's playtime enlivened by piano and strings, then a final round of races.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playtime' reads as one word but must be split. The P lands just after the first letter of the instruments. 'Heats' are not races but fires.
explanation.definitionFit: Funeral pyres are the fires on which bodies are cremated, so they are the last heat a person meets.

clue.text: ... was successful about greeting in pseudo-French, not Flemish

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for success wraps around the greeting

blocks.note: won is the past tense of win
a mock-French hello, as in the British sitcom 'Allo 'Allo!

explanation.surface: Continuing 9: someone succeeded in a fake French accent and so wasn't from Flanders.
explanation.walkthrough: W-ALLO-ON: the greeting sits inside WON. 'Allo 'Allo! was a BBC comedy set in wartime France with comic French accents.
explanation.definitionFit: Walloons are the French-speaking people of southern Belgium, contrasted with the Dutch-speaking Flemish of the north.

clue.text: River of silence, with name among the nameless

indicators.note: among places one item in the middle of a group, so a letter goes inside

blocks.note: the hushing sound used to call for quiet
anon is short for anonymous
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A quiet river, its name unknown to everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The nameless' are anonymous people, abbreviated as in the signature on an unattributed poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shannon is the longest river in Ireland, flowing south-west to the Atlantic.

clue.text: Grandma pregnant? She must be kidding!

blocks.note: first meaning: a familiar British name for a grandmother
second meaning: a female goat expecting young goats

explanation.surface: Someone hears that their gran is expecting and assumes it must be a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kidding' looks like joking, but it means giving birth to kids, young goats.
explanation.definitionFit: Nanny is a childish word for grandmother, and a nanny goat is the female, which bears kids.

clue.text: Resident's home with Dickens's leader and servant

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter standing at its front

blocks.note: being at home is being in
the opening letter of the novelist's name
Sam Weller is Mr Pickwick's servant in Dickens's The Pickwick Papers

explanation.surface: A householder lives with a Dickens character and his servant.
explanation.walkthrough: The servant is a Dickens one: Sam Weller from The Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: An indweller is someone who dwells within a place, an inhabitant, which is what a resident is.

clue.text: Wife and child I leave in agricultural building

indicators.note: the letter I departs, so it is taken out of the word for the child

blocks.note: 'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for a man's wife
bairn is Scots and northern English for a child

explanation.surface: A man's wife and child are left behind on a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My old Dutch' is Cockney for wife; take the I out of BAIRN to leave BARN.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dutch barn is a farm shed with a curved roof on open sides, used for storing hay.

clue.text: Application for cooking meat in church council

indicators.note: cooking means altering something, so the meat letters are mixed into a new order
in puts the mixed letters inside the name of the council

blocks.note: the Council of Trent was the sixteenth-century Catholic council
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A church committee has applied to cook some meat.
explanation.walkthrough: TRE-ATME-NT: the rearranged meat goes inside TRENT.
explanation.definitionFit: An application of an ointment or remedy is a treatment, a medical sense of the word.

clue.text: He slept, wrongly, with Scots girl

indicators.note: wrongly means not in the right order, so the letters must be put another way

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man slept with a Scottish girl when he shouldn't have.
explanation.definitionFit: Elspeth is the Scottish form of Elizabeth, a girl's name common north of the border.

clue.text: Following notes in following part-exchange

indicators.note: in places the notes inside the second word for a following, so it surrounds them

blocks.note: a train is a retinue, the following of a great person
two musical notes, D and E

explanation.surface: A puzzling list of follow-ups in a car-dealing deal.
explanation.walkthrough: TRA-DE-IN: notes D and E go inside TRAIN. The opening 'Following' only joins; it says the definition comes after the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade-in is an old item handed over as partial payment for a new one, which is what part-exchange means.

clue.text: Nick a second duck

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
the teal is a small wild duck

explanation.surface: Pinch a second duck from the pond.
explanation.walkthrough: To nick is British slang for to steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick is everyday British slang for pinching or taking without permission, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Romance in a long dress was said to have finished Mozart

definitions.text: was said to have finished Mozart

indicators.note: in places the romance inside the garment, which wraps around it

blocks.note: the sari is a long wrapped garment worn in South Asia
to romance is to tell fanciful untruths

explanation.surface: A love affair conducted in a long gown, with Mozart's end hinted at.
explanation.walkthrough: SA-LIE-RI: the untruth goes inside SARI. 'Finished' means killed, not completed.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio Salieri was the rival composer rumoured, without evidence, to have poisoned Mozart.

clue.text: Back at last - steed wouldn't start

indicators.note: failing to start means the word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: the end comes at last
a steed is a horse

explanation.surface: A rider finally returns because the horse refused to get going.
explanation.walkthrough: END plus HORSE without its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To back a plan or person is to support it, which is what endorse means.

clue.text: I - my husband also - need break with continuity

definitions.text: I - my husband also - need break with continuity

blocks.clueFragment: I - my husband also - need break
blocks.note: surface: a weary wife says both she and her husband need time away
setter's reading: time off spent doing much the same as one's job, so the work goes on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Break with continuity' looks like a clean break from the past, but it is a break in which work carries on.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names leisure time spent doing the same sort of thing as your usual work, as a bus driver taking a coach trip.

clue.text: What makes widows at 10 good enough?

blocks.note: satis, or suttees, are widows burned on their husbands' funeral pyres
a factory is where things are made

explanation.surface: A grim question about a supply of widows for the pyres of 10.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 refers to 10 Down. Sati (suttee) was the old Hindu practice of a widow burning herself on her husband's pyre; the word also names the widow.
explanation.definitionFit: Satisfactory means adequate or acceptable, meeting the standard required without excelling.

clue.text: See 21
Ancient city time insufficient, I'm afraid, among single characters at liberty: we purchase only seconds

annotation.answer: THE BEST THINGS IN LIFE ARE FREE

indicators.note: characters here are loose letters to be dealt out afresh rather than read as the word they now spell

blocks.note: Thebes was a great city of ancient Egypt and also of ancient Greece
T is the abbreviation for time
a thin supply is an insufficient one
the setter's loose step: the I of I'm with the F of afraid, a hedging if
taken as written
people at liberty are free, read as the words are free

explanation.surface: An apologetic shopkeeper among ancient ruins explains that, time being short, only second-quality goods are on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: Most of the wordplay is clean, but the IF from 'I'm afraid' has no standard device behind it; treat it as Araucaria's liberty. The definition is a joke: if the best things are free, what we pay for is second best.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying holds that the finest pleasures cost nothing, so anything bought must be second-rate goods.
